items.prompt: A photo app stores 100 million new 2 MB images a day, keeps them forever, and must never lose one after the upload is acknowledged. Where do the image bytes go?
items.why: Write-once binary data at hundreds of TB a day with high durability needs → object storage. The database only keeps the metadata and the key; the CDN only delivers copies.

items.prompt: Viewers in Asia wait 400 ms for the first byte of popular product videos that live in a single US region.
items.why: The data is already stored; the problem is distance to many readers of the same public files → edge delivery from a CDN, with object storage as the origin.

items.prompt: Mobile clients upload videos of up to 10 GB, and you don't want those bytes passing through your API servers. How does the API let a client write exactly one key for 15 minutes?
items.why: The question is about authorising one operation on one object for a short time, not about where it's stored → a presigned URL.

items.prompt: A 20 GB backup upload over a flaky hotel connection keeps failing at 90% and starting over from zero.
items.why: This is the object store's multipart upload: parts are sent in parallel, a failed part is retried on its own, and complete assembles them by part number.

items.prompt: Thousands of users keep the same 300 MB installer in their accounts, and a small edit to a big file currently re-uploads the whole thing.
items.why: Sharing identical bytes and sending only what changed is about how files are split and matched by content hash. The object store just holds the parts.

items.prompt: The design needs somewhere to put large binary files outside the database; the interviewer asks which managed service you would actually use and what its per-request limits are.
items.why: Naming the concrete service (S3/GCS), its PUT size cap, multipart, prefixes and tiers is the object-storage topic; blob storage is the general idea behind it.

items.prompt: A shopping cart is read and updated by key on every click and must respond in under 5 ms.
items.why: Small, mutable values with millisecond latency are an anti-signal for object storage (immutable objects, tens of ms to first byte) → a key-value store.

items.prompt: A crawler fetches 2 billion HTML pages a month and must keep the raw pages for 6 months so another team can reprocess them in bulk.
items.why: Hundreds of TB of write-once documents, read back whole in batch jobs → object storage, cheap per GB and with lifecycle rules to expire them.
